Mr. President, France welcomes the adoption of resolution 2467 (2019), submitted by Germany, which we thank for its initiative. This resolution constitutes a significant milestone in our collective action on women, peace and security, reaffirming the framework established in resolutions 1889 (2009) and 2106 (2013). It strengthens the mandate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict, Ms. Pramila Patten, and adopts a survivor-centred approach. We specifically support the request that the Secretary-General produce a report on children born out of rape by 2021.

However, we must acknowledge that important concessions were made under pressure from several permanent members. We deplore the removal of the reference to sexual and reproductive health, previously agreed upon in resolutions 1889 and 2106. It is unacceptable that access to such care is omitted for victims of atrocities, undermining their dignity. France maintains that women must decide freely about their own bodies, including the right to terminate involuntary pregnancies, and will continue to promote full access to sexual and reproductive health care in every context.

Regarding the hypothetical application P, which calls itself survivor-centred but withholds care until a final conviction, we note that parallel care and justice require immediate access. We recommend revising such proposals to provide comprehensive sexual and reproductive care without a conviction gate, while funding a survivor-referral route for care and a separate voluntary protected referral route for investigation. Waiting for conviction harms access. These are analytical recommendations for this exercise, not an official endorsement of P or a future vote.

On behalf of France, I renew our call to continue the fight against sexual violence in conflict.<|im_end|>

On behalf of the United Kingdom, I extend congratulations to Germany for the successful adoption of resolution 2467 (2019). While I attach myself to the achievements highlighted by my French colleague, I must also acknowledge the significant steps remaining to ensure survivors are truly at the heart of our approach. The resolution recognizes a survivor-centred approach, the disproportionate impact of conflict-related sexual violence on women and girls, and the vital role of civil society. However, we deeply regret the omission of language regarding services for survivors, specifically the exclusion of comprehensive reproductive and sexual health care. This omission contradicts the acute need for such services.

The UK will continue to support access to sexual and reproductive health care for survivors of sexual violence around the world; this remains a priority. A genuine survivor-centred approach cannot ignore this essential component. Furthermore, while we welcome the adoption, we recognize that more steps are required to achieve true justice and accountability.

Regarding the hypothetical application P, which proposes withholding care until a final conviction, I offer the following analytical recommendation for this exercise: P should be revised to provide immediate comprehensive sexual and reproductive care without a conviction gate. Additionally, a survivor-referral route for care and a separate voluntary protected referral route for investigation or prosecution should be funded. Parallel care and justice require staffing and coordination, but waiting for conviction harms access.

This recommendation does not constitute an official endorsement of P or an established future vote. The record confirms the UK's real, ongoing commitment to survivor care, but no unspecified future text or vote has been adopted.<|im_end|>
